title.narrative: Plan International Sverige Digital Skills 4 Youth 2023-2026
Plan International Sweden Digital Skills 4 Youth 2023-2026

description.narrative: Ansökan om finansieringsstöd från Plan International Sverige för ett projekt med titeln ”Digital Skills 4 Youth Project 2023-2026”, syftar till att utforma ett program för ungdomars anställbarhet och entreprenörskap underbyggt av digitala färdigheter med olika tvärsektoriella och urban-landsbygdskopplingar.

The application for funding support by Plan International Sweden for a project titled Digital Skills 4 Youth Project 2023-2026, seeks to model a youth employability and entrepreneurship programme underpinned by digital skills with various cross-sectoral and urban-rural linkages.

The broad outcome of the proposal is to enhance sustainable, productive economic development for youth, particularly young women in a supportive environment for digital skills entrepreneurship and employment in targeted areas. The intervention has identified outcomes as key in achieving the set objective:
Outcome 1
1,680 young people, including young women in the targeted areas have strengthened skills relevant for the digital labour market. An additional 3000 young people will be reached under the virtual market intervention.
Outcome 2
Targeted areas have strengthened structures for young people's professional development including linkages with the digital labour market, especially for young women
Outcome 3
Private and governmental sectors on a national and local level have taken actions to enhance young womens economic rights and economic participation
Young women in Zimbabwe face high rates of unemployment coupled with its negative effects including lack of livelihood, and high rates of negative coping mechanisms (e.g. crime, drug abuse and risky health behaviours). There is a huge digital divide in Zimbabwe that cannot be ignored if digital skills programmes are to be truly equitable. Thus, the intervention is expected to impact young peoples digital skills, enabling their sustainable income-generation through either entrepreneurship or employment.
The project offers two streams of digital skills interventions; that is, tailored for rural and urban youth. It is envisaged that the basic digital skills stream coupled with the MakerSpace model (physical work spaces equipped to provide technical training on agro-processing that incorporates basic digital skills) will enable rural youth to perform ICT-enhanced trade through entrepreneurship or employment; whilst the intermediate/advanced digital skills stream coupled with the job market linkages will enhance urban youths employability or entrepreneurship in the digital economy.
Revised Priority Areas
The programme will concentrate on the following key areas:
Scalability of Business Interventions Supporting initiatives that can be expanded and replicated to reach a wider audience and deliver long-term impact.
Hub Sustainability Strengthening innovation and resource hubs to ensure their operational viability and ability to serve communities beyond the programmes lifespan.
Entrepreneurship Development Building entrepreneurial capacity through targeted training and support, enabling individuals to create and grow businesses.
Job Linkages Enhancing connections between skills development, entrepreneurship, and employment opportunities to improve livelihoods.
It is Sidas assessment that, the reduced budget necessitates a sharper focus on interventions that are proven to deliver measurable results and that this approach prioritizes activities with the highest potential for impact, ensuring that every investment contributes directly to achieving sustainable outcomes.

The programme has led to significant improvements in digital literacy, employability, and economic participation among young people, particularly young women. Through targeted training, mentorship, and linkages with innovation hubs and private sector actors, youth who previously had limited access to digital tools are now able to apply practical digital skills in real-world contexts. Participants have transitioned from basic or no exposure to technology to actively using digital platforms for communication, content creation, job searching, and income generation. A substantial proportion of trained youth have moved into internships, freelancing, and small-scale entrepreneurship, indicating progress toward the programmes objective of enhancing youth livelihoods.
A key transformation has been observed in the increased confidence, agency, and aspirations of participants. Young people are now better equipped to navigate digital environments, collaborate professionally, and pursue opportunities within the digital economy. For many, especially young women, this represents a shift from social and economic exclusion to active participation. Female participants have not only taken part in large numbers but have also demonstrated strong completion and engagement rates, contributing to narrowing gender gaps in access to digital skills. The programme has also contributed to changing community perceptions, with greater acceptance of girls involvement in technology and income-generating activities.
The intervention has influenced the practices and priorities of ecosystem actors. Training institutions and implementing partners have adopted more inclusive, hands-on, and market-relevant approaches to digital skills development. Private sector actors have increasingly engaged in mentorship, internship placements, and collaboration with training providers, reflecting stronger linkages between skills development and labour market needs. In addition, partners have shown commitment to sustaining elements of the programme beyond the project cycle, suggesting early signs of institutionalisation and potential for scale.
Behavioural changes among the target group are evident. Youth are not only acquiring skills but also applying themlaunching small digital enterprises, offering ICT-related services, and continuing to pursue learning opportunities. Some participants have demonstrated resilience by continuing to engage with digital work despite resource constraints. Overall, the programme has contributed to enhanced capabilities, increased economic participation, and gradual shifts in gender norms, making a meaningful contribution in a context characterised by high youth unemployment and digital exclusion.
Despite these achievements, several challenges have limited the full realisation and scaling of results. Structural barriersparticularly limited access to affordable internet, digital devices, and reliable electricityhave constrained the ability of many participants to consistently practice and monetise their skills. A significant proportion of youth, especially young women, do not own personal devices and rely on shared or public resources, reducing continuity in learning and income generation. High data costs further restricted access to online platforms, limiting participation in digital work opportunities.
Gender disparities, although reduced, persist and continue to affect outcomes. Young women face disproportionate barriers, including unpaid care responsibilities, mobility constraints, and entrenched socio-cultural norms that limit sustained participation in training and employment. While female enrolment and completion rates are strong, the transition to income-generating activities remains more difficult for women than for men. Occupational segregation within the digital sector and limited access to networks, finance, and safe working environments further hinder womens ability to fully benefit from acquired skills.
Labour market constraints also affected the programmes outcomes. While participants gained relevant and market-aligned skills, the availability of decent employment opportunities in the local economy remains limited. Private sector absorption capacity is relatively low, and competition for digital jobs is high, making it difficult for all graduates to secure stable income streams. This gap between skills acquisition and employment outcomes highlights broader systemic issues that extend beyond the scope of the intervention.
Retention and sustained engagement of participants presented additional challenges. Some youth dropped out or reduced participation due to financial pressures, competing livelihood needs, or household responsibilities. This was particularly evident among vulnerable groups who prioritised immediate income over longer-term skills development. In some cases, participants struggled to maintain motivation where immediate economic returns were not visible, affecting the depth and sustainability of impact.
Finally, while partner institutions demonstrated commitment, capacity constraints and resource limitations affected the pace and scale of implementation. Expanding successful models to reach more youth or deepen support (e.g., through advanced training, incubation, or job placement) was limited by funding, infrastructure, and operational challenges. These constraints highlight the need for complementary investments and stronger ecosystem support to fully realise the programmes potential.
